doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Producer Mat Domber, overdub awareness and Nola studio
summary: Mat Domber's laid-back production, being respectful as a sideman, mental notes for overdubs, and engineer Jimmy Czak at Nola.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: How much control do you get over — I mean you have a producer whose in a sense paying for the session?
It depends who the producer is.
Who says, “Well I like take 1, and he likes take 2.”

Mat is pretty cool. Mat is very cool. He is so laid back. He’s like oh it all sounds good to me. He’s pretty much that. You know what I mean? But sometimes he really has an opinion about it, it’s like, “I like that.” “No, the other one’s better.” Sometimes he will actually say what he likes. It’s generally up to the band leader on those sessions. So often I’m hearing on a bass solo like oh, I hope they don’t keep this track. But they’ll say keep this track, and I’m not the leader, I have to — because it’s a time thing. So if the gig, if you’re not the leader on the session, you can’t be tying up people’s time, like, “I want to do that bass solo again, I don’t like it.” You know you can’t be tying up people’s time that way. Do you know what I mean? You have to be respectful, it’s their record. If they’re happy with it or if they didn’t like it they could say to you, “Why don’t you run the first four bars of that, you didn’t sound so great” you know what I mean? The other thing I’ll do in a session, because I do love recording and I love — you know I don’t like wasting time. I don’t like too much talking time or eating time or, you now. I like to, you know, like let’s get to it. Because you do it on a roll. When you’re doing a take, I find that you really have to be aware of, because it’s tiny, four hours and four hours, well rock records get done in six months. You know what I mean? I mean you really have to be aware of if you make a mistake or you don’t make the right changes at a point or you miss the ending or you didn’t even make the beginning. You have to make a mental alert as you go through the tape. And you can say, at the end of the tape, I need to overdub bars 16 and 17. You know what I mean? Because they may not be hearing it if someone’s talking and they don’t hear it, then they get the product and they come up and say, “Oh, what happened to Nicki there? Oh, she missed that.” But if you make a mental note you

can say listen I need to overdub these bars and I know I was nowhere near it. So that’s another good thing in the studio I think is to be aware of it in terms of — because that might be the take they pick.
Then they can actually punch you in for a couple of bars.

Exactly. While they’re recording it’s incredible. I have to thank Les for that, multi-track recording. So it’s fast, it’s easy — and working with engineers like Jimmy Czak up at Nola who does almost all of my New York recording.
Boy that place has been there for a long time.
And often Jimmy will hear it, Jimmy is like, “Nicki, play the ending again, it wasn’t clean.” “You’re right.” Bam. It really takes like not even two minutes. It’s amazingly fast now.
That place has been there a long time.
I mean I remember guys that played in the 30s I think. Maybe not that long. But it must be neat to be in that kind of a place, like Milt Hinton played here.

It’s just a good energy. It’s a great energy up there. It really is. It’s always a nice vibe. It’s funny, it’s not too serious. Sometimes it gets serious if someone’s not happy with the music or the musicians or something, but really generally it’s a good time. People pop in all the time. It’s a great energy.
